title: School-Related Words
description: The lesson that hands out the vocabulary the whole education unit will be argued in: the ladder a pupil climbs (primary school, secondary school, the Ordinary papers behind the O of O level and the Advanced papers behind the A of A level, then university), the verb attend that takes its object with no preposition and must never be confused with assisting somebody, the year cut into three terms or into two semesters and printed week by week on the timetable, the headings that gather the subjects (the sciences over physics, chemistry and biology, languages over English, French and German, with geometry and art under neither), the four operations said out loud (add, subtract, multiply, divide) and the everyday phrases that hide them, everything printed on a page from the book down through the chapter, the paragraph, the sentence and the full stop, with the margin left blank down the side, the examination room where a candidate faces an examiner and where written and oral do not mean practical and theoretical, the twelve pairs of opposites of the field (teach/learn, clever/stupid, pass/fail, attend/leave, worse/better, work/holiday) and the two rules the box never prints - an opposite answers a meaning and not a word, so the same adjective takes different opposites in different sentences, and an adverb takes no opposite from the adjective's list; then word building with the spidergram (provide/provision, deny/denial, reduce/reduction, attend/attendance, expect/expectation/expectant), the four endings and the warning that none of them can be guessed or invented, the nouns that newspapers build their headlines on, the five new words boost, deny, nutritious, priority and provide with the two senses of deny and the rank that priority really names, how an advertisement is taken apart - headline, subtitle, body, appeal, contact details - how the paratext lets you predict the body and how the tail of a web address and the first word of an e-mail address name the sender, what persuasion adds to information, the chain of consequences a good appeal shows and the danger of reading it backwards, and finally the structure too + adjective + to, which carries its own negative, blocks where very only measures, hands the second verb to whoever is named after for, and can just as well praise as blame
